newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Thistle to give Brierley big warchest.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Thistle to give Brierley big warchest.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd will be provided with a sizeable warchest from the selldown of its Thistle Hotels holding and it is on the warpath to use it, Chief Executive Paul Collins said on Thursday.

"Today we could invest quite comfortably NZ$750 million without placing any pressure on the group in any way, shape or form," he said in an interview shortly after BIL reported a $310 million June year net profit, down from $432 million.
"With the selldown of Thistle Hotels that number would rise up to NZ$1.5 billion."
BIL has said it wants to cut its stake below 50 percent from 70 percent when the British hotel group floats next month but has not specified a target. It will depend on price and market conditions.
"If the market is very strong and very supportive you might see a higher level of selldown. We are going to have a shareholding of 35 to 50 percent of the enlarged capital."
Thistle, which has been a millstone around BIL's neck since purchased in 1990, is still the company's biggest asset and the biggest determinant on its share price.
Collins rejected selling out completely. He says the British hotel market is buoyant, leaving plenty of room for growth.
However, by floating Thistle, the true market value will be realised and Thistle's share price should head northward as the company is better understood and improves earnings again.
"Whatever value it is brought to market, assuming normal market conditions, the share price will go up in value."
Collins also rejected the idea of a BIL capital reduction, suggested by some analysts as an alternative use for the cash.

If the value of BIL suddenly appreciated or if all of Thistle was sold, it might create excess of capital, but Collins said BIL had canvassed that issue thoroughly last year and maintains holding onto the cash is currently the best option.

"At this stage none of the stakes we put in the ground last year have come to pass. We still see significant investment opportunities out there and we don't believe the level of capital is inappropriate for the size of the group."

BIL expects to exercise some of its investment plans through Delham Investments, a powerful grouping of Asian investors which took 20 percent of BIL in March and which has been offered two places on the BIL board. The investment was subsequently backed into Malex Industries Bhd.
Collins denied he had grabbed a tiger by the tail with Delham, saying the pair planned to undertake "co-investment-type" opportunites in Australasia and Asia.
"There will be areas we can mutually work on together and I have got no doubt over the next year to 18 months there will be things we do do together."
He said Delham was interested in gaining exposure to Australian industrial-type companies exposed to Asian growth.
"I'm totally relaxed about their involvement," he said.
BIL recently revealed it had spend NZ$280 million accumulating a stake in Australian retailer Coles Myer.
But he was extemely coy on giving further details.
"We are not going to say anything more publicly about it. We don't like sharing with the market for obvious reasons our strategy on listed public company investment."
He was equally coy on other recently revealed investments such as a four percent stake in Fletcher Energy.
But he was not shy stating Australia was a prime target.
"It is an important market and there will be continuing investment there."
BIL sees the investment field clear of similar competitors in Australasia, with most 1980s rivals having disappeared.
Chairman Bob Matthew said earlier that the year had started well for BIL and despite a slowdown in New Zealand, he expected operating earnings in 1996/97 to be satisfactory.
"We don't see any great turnaround in New Zealand over the next 12 months -- we see conditions being a bit difficult, some of the businesses performing well and some averagely," Collins said.
Collins, who took up his post in December 1985 at the tender age of 32, said he was content in his job. "I have no plans to make any changes." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
